title: Whose Story Is It?
subtitle: A memoir says: this is what happened. But memory edits, and one voice is only one voice. How do you talk about whether a true story can be trusted — and disagree without falling out?

card.who: Marjane Satrapi · and a war story that admits it was partly invented
card.essence: What a memoir can promise and what it cannot, why a story can feel truer than a list of facts, and the polite phrases for disagreeing in a group.

intention: you'll discuss whether a true story can be trusted, using a three-step check, and practise the language of polite disagreement — so you can argue a point in a group without losing the room.
warmup: Think of a family story you have heard many times. How sure are you it happened exactly that way?
If two people remember the same event differently, can both be telling the truth? How?
Do you trust a memoir more or less than a history book? Why?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: Her recollection of the evening was vivid, but her brother remembered it completely differently.
items.meaning: recollection (noun) — a memory of something; the act of remembering.

items.sent: Some storytellers embellish: they add small, colourful details that never happened to make the story better.
items.meaning: embellish (verb) — to make a story more interesting by adding extra or invented details.

items.sent: A credible witness is someone you can believe because they have no reason to lie and their details fit together.
Every memoirist has some bias: a natural leaning towards their own version of events.
items.meaning: bias (noun) — a tendency to see or present things from one particular point of view.

vocab.heading: B · Weighing a personal account
vocab.intro: Same method: guess from the sentence, then reveal.

items.sent: Her testimony carried weight because she had seen the events herself.
items.meaning: testimony (noun) — a statement of what a person saw or experienced, offered as evidence.

items.sent: Memory is selective: it keeps some moments sharply and loses others entirely.
items.meaning: selective (adjective) — choosing only some things and leaving others out.

items.sent: Readers value the authentic voice of a memoir: the sense that someone is really speaking, not performing.
items.meaning: authentic (adjective) — genuine; real and not copied or invented.

vocab.heading: C · Joining the debate
vocab.intro: Three words for arguing about a book. Guess, then reveal.

items.sent: After so many years she found it hard to retell the story the same way twice.
items.meaning: retell (verb) — to tell a story again, often in a new or changed way.

items.sent: I can't vouch for every detail, but I trust the spirit of what she says.
items.meaning: vouch for (verb) — to say that you know something is true or that someone is reliable.

items.sent: Whether the book speaks for a whole country is contested: readers disagree sharply.
items.meaning: contested (adjective) — argued about; not agreed by everyone.

vocab_use: Describe a story from your own life that you have retold so often that it has changed. How?
Whose testimony would you trust first on a difficult subject — and why?
Name something that is contested among your friends or family. How do people argue about it?
story_heading: When the true story and the real story are not the same

story.heading: Part 1 — The promise of a memoir
paras: A memoir makes a promise to the reader: this happened, and I was there. That promise is its power. Readers of Persepolis know they are not reading an invention. They are reading what a real woman says she lived through, in a country most of them have never seen from the inside.

But the promise is harder to keep than it sounds. The author must draw on a recollection of events decades old, and memory does not work like a camera. It is selective: it forgets, repairs and rearranges. She must also rebuild conversations and decide what to draw: how a room looked, what people wore, exactly what was said.

There is another puzzle. In a graphic memoir the author draws herself: a child, a teenager, then a young woman. She is both the person telling the story and the person the story is about, and she has chosen how to draw that person.
checks: Why is it hard to keep that promise?
What is unusual about the author's role in a graphic memoir?
answers: That the events really happened and the author was there.
Because memory is selective: it forgets, repairs and rearranges, and conversations must be rebuilt.
She is both the person telling the story and the character she has chosen how to draw.
story.discuss: If a writer changes the order of events or invents the exact words of a conversation, is the memoir still true?

story.heading: Part 2 — Story-truth and happening-truth
paras: The American writer Tim O'Brien, who fought in Vietnam, wrote a book called The Things They Carried (1990) that sits between memoir and fiction. The narrator is called Tim, like the author, and the stories feel like true war stories — yet the book admits that some of what we read is invented.

O'Brien's narrator makes a bold argument. There is "happening-truth", what actually occurred, and there is "story-truth", the truth of how it felt and what it meant. Sometimes, he says, the second can be more honest than the first. A list of what a soldier carried says little about what it was like to carry it.

Persepolis takes a different path. It claims to be true, and it is told in a simple, controlled voice. But it faces the same question: when someone tells a painful story, what matters most — the exact words that were spoken, or the feeling a reader can be made to share?
checks: What kind of book is The Things They Carried?
What is the difference between happening-truth and story-truth?
How does Persepolis face the same question?
answers: A book between memoir and fiction, with a narrator named after the author and some invented material.
Happening-truth is what actually occurred; story-truth is the truth of how it felt and what it meant.
It claims to be true, but it must decide whether exact facts or shared feeling matters more.
story.discuss: Can a story that contains something invented still be truthful? Give an example.

story.heading: Part 3 — Reading a true story with care
paras: A personal account is testimony: one witness saying what she saw. That is its value. It lets readers feel history through one life instead of through statistics. But it also has limits. One person's view is always partial, and no memoir can speak for a whole country. Readers have asked, quite fairly: whose Iran is this? One family, one class, one time.

For that reason, careful readers do two things at once. They treat the author as credible, because she has a reason to be honest and the details fit together. And they notice bias: the choices about what to include, and the way her own feelings colour the story.

A memoir works best when we treat it as a window rather than a mirror of the whole truth: a real view from a real place, to be set beside other voices. Its authentic quality does not come from being complete. It comes from being honest about what one person knew.
checks: What makes a memoir valuable as testimony?
How should a careful reader read a memoir?
answers: It lets readers feel history through one real life instead of statistics.
It is one partial view and cannot speak for a whole country.
With trust in the author's honesty, but also noticing her choices and bias, and setting her voice beside others.
story.discuss: Whose voice should we hear first if we want to understand a war: a historian, a soldier or a child? Why?

tool_tab.lead: When someone tells you a true story, you are being asked to trust three different things at once. The Truth Check separates them, so you can say what you accept, what you question and why.
how: Facts. What could be checked against dates, records or other witnesses? If it is checkable, check it, or say you have not.
Feelings. What was it like for the person? You cannot check a feeling, but you can ask whether it is believable and whether it matches the facts.
Voice. Who is telling the story, and what are they choosing to include? Whose view is missing? Is the voice trying to persuade you?
Round again. A new fact can change your reading of a feeling, and a new voice can change your reading of both. Keep going round.

sort.intro: Each sentence could be said about a memoir. Which step of the Truth Check is it about?

items.text: The school became single-sex in the early 1980s.
items.why: a claim that records could confirm.

items.text: She says she felt as if everyone in the street was watching her.
She is writing as an adult looking back, so she chooses which memories to include.
items.why: it concerns who is telling and what they choose.

items.text: The war with Iraq began in September 1980.
The panic she describes rings true: it matches what other people report from that time.
items.why: it judges whether a feeling is believable.

items.text: One family's story cannot speak for a whole country.
items.why: it asks whose voice is represented.

items.text: The dates she gives for her move to Vienna fit with the other events she describes.
Her grief on those pages is clearly sincere, even if some details may be reconstructed.
items.why: it judges the honesty of an emotion.

breaks: The steps overlap. One sentence can contain a fact, a feeling and a choice. Pull them apart before you judge.
Unchecked is not false. Many true things cannot be verified. The right response is care, not dismissal.
Everyone has a voice. You are never reading from nowhere, and neither is the author. Ask what you bring to the page, too.
discuss: Which step do you tend to skip when you read a memoir?
Can a memoir be trusted on feeling if it is weak on facts?

grammar.name: Disagreeing politely
grammar.lead: A book club is a place where people disagree and stay friends. The language of polite disagreement — conceding a point, softening an objection and holding your position — is a skill in its own right.
notes: 1 · Concede first. Show you have heard the other view before you add yours: “That's a fair point, but…” “I take your point; even so…” “I see what you mean, although…”
2 · Soften the objection. “I'm not sure I agree.” “I'd put it slightly differently.” “I wonder whether…” Avoid That's wrong and You're mistaken.
3 · Hold your ground. You do not have to give way: “I still think…” “Even so, it seems to me that…” “I hear you, but I'd argue…”
4 · Agree strongly. “I couldn't agree more.” “Absolutely — that was the part that stayed with me.” Agreement should add something, not just repeat.
5 · Interrupt and clarify. “Sorry to jump in…” “Do you mean…?” “I think I put that badly — what I meant was…”
6 · Traps. I don't agree with you alone sounds blunt; add a reason or a softener. I take your point, but I think so → “I take your point, but I still think it's more complicated.”

exercises.heading: Choose the most diplomatic reply
exercises.intro: Choose the reply that would work best in a friendly book discussion.
items: 1. Someone says: "The ending was perfect." You partly disagree. (a) "That's wrong." (b) "I see what you mean, although I wanted a bit more." (c) "Whatever." → ___

2. Someone says: "The author exaggerates; it can't all be true." (a) "Nobody exaggerates in a memoir." (b) "You're being silly." (c) "Fair point, but I'd say the feeling is true even if details change." → ___
3. You want to add something while someone is speaking. (a) "Sorry to jump in — could I add something?" (b) "Stop talking." (c) "Yes yes, but listen." → ___
4. Someone has misunderstood you. (a) "You didn't listen." (b) "That's not what I said." (c) "I think I put that badly — what I meant was…" → ___
5. You strongly agree with someone. (a) "No." (b) "I couldn't agree more — that was the part that stayed with me." (c) "Maybe." → ___
answers: 1. (b)
2. (c)
3. (a)
4. (c)
5. (b)

exercises.heading: Soften it
exercises.intro: Each statement is too blunt for a book club. Rewrite it more politely, keeping the same view. (Model answers are suggestions.)
items: 3. No, the book is not trustworthy.
answers: 1. I'm not sure I agree about the ending; I saw it rather differently.
2. I'd put it slightly differently — it seems to me the author means something else.
3. I take your point, but I'm not convinced the book is fully trustworthy.
4. I think I put that badly — what I meant was a bit different.

exercises.heading: Complete the phrase
exercises.intro: Write one word in each gap.
items: 1. I ___ your point, but I think it's more complicated.
2. I see ___ you mean, although I read it differently.
3. I'm not ___ I agree with that.
4. That's a fair ___, but I'd argue the opposite.
answers: 1. take
2. what
3. sure
4. point
5. agree

grammar.closing: Now disagree politely with a view you have heard this week, using one concession, one softener and one way of holding your ground.

speak.intro: Now it's your turn. Choose a task, start the timer and talk. On your own it works as a talk; with a partner or a group, take turns and respond to each other.
speak.useful: “That's a fair point, but…” · “I'd put it slightly differently…” · “I take your point; even so…” · “What can be checked is… what can't is…” · “Whose voice is missing?”

tasks.label: Task 1 — A story that changed
paras: Tell us a story you have told so many times that it has changed. What did you add, drop or smooth over?

tasks.label: Task 2 — The Truth Check
paras: Choose a memoir, a documentary or a news report. Run the three steps: facts, feelings and voice.

tasks.label: Task 3 — Trust it or not?
paras: A friend says a memoir can never be trusted. Respond using at least two phrases of polite disagreement.

tasks.label: Task 4 — Story-truth
paras: Is it ever acceptable to change facts to tell a deeper truth? Defend a position, then give the best opposing point.

final: A memoir is told by the person it is about. Does that make it more trustworthy, or less?
If one witness cannot speak for a country, what is the reader's responsibility?
What would be missing from our picture of the world if only checkable facts were allowed?
From memory: name the three steps of the Truth Check and one polite way to disagree.
